paragraphs.text: Dear sisters and elders, I hope you're all doing well this evening. We've had a great mission president seminar this week. We had to use Zoom, like we do our own conferences, district and interviews and so forth, but it was still very uplifting and edifying. We had a special blessing in having President Dallin H. Oaks, the first counselor in the First Presidency, join us for our very first session. He taught us for about two hours, so that was great. And we had Elder D. Todd Christofferson and Elder Carl B. Cook for two of our sessions, so it was great to be taught by all of them.

It was a blessing and I hope to be able to share some of those things with you in our upcoming Zoom conferences. It was also great to be taught by our area presidency. These are all fine, fine, fine men and each of them and their wonderful wives asked us to pass along their love and blessings to you, to each of you.

Tonight, I'd like to share some thoughts with you from the story of Joseph, the son of Jacob and the father of Manasseh and Ephraim. Most of us in this mission are from either the tribe of Manasseh or Ephraim, which means that pretty much all of us are from Joseph. And this is a great blessing because Joseph was an amazing, amazing man. He was a prophet in every sense of the word, but more than that, he literally changed the future of Israel because of his work.

The Lord set him up to do a great work, and as it is usually the case, the way the Lord sets us up is sometimes with challenging experiences. And that was certainly the case for Joseph. He had a very challenging life. He started out in life as kind of a favorite of his father, and that really irritated his older brothers, so much so that they decided to secretly kill him. Then one of the brothers persuaded the others to sell him as a slave to a traveling caravan of merchants, and so that's what they did instead.

Joseph ended up in Egypt and he was sold by the merchants to a man of the name of Potiphar. Now Potiphar was the captain of the Pharaoh's guards and a very powerful and fearsome man. Potiphar was very soon impressed with this young slave that he had bought. He was impressed with the intelligence and the diligence of Joseph and probably the great attitude that he manifested. He quickly promoted Joseph to be over all the management of his entire household.

So there are a couple of things to note about this development. The first one is that Joseph obviously didn't mope or whine or complain about his bad luck being sold as a slave. I mean, he could have spent all his time just doing the minimal work and complaining about how bad he had been treated by his family. If he had, he would not have impressed Potiphar and he would have stayed a lowly slave. Second, he was clearly not just smart but he was also very honest and very hard in his work ethic. If he hadn't been those things, a man of Potiphar's stature and intelligence would never have placed him in a position that he placed him in as being the manager of his whole household.

So again, now things are starting to look up again for Joseph. And then of course Potiphar's wife tries to get him to violate the law of chastity and in the process to betray his master and his God. As you all know, Joseph resisted, and this went on for quite a while. This just wasn't a one-time thing. She tried this again and again and again. We learned that it went on for a long time as we read carefully in that scripture. He finally had to resist a rather aggressive attempt on her part and he literally had to flee, and she captured a piece of his clothing which tore off and kept that.

Now, Joseph's a smart man—he knows how this is going to end and it's not going to end well for him. But he still wouldn't violate his own integrity and the commandments of God or his trust that Potiphar had given to him, even knowing that when Potiphar heard from his wife, he wouldn't believe anything that Joseph had or would say. And sure enough, Potiphar's wife told her husband that Joseph had tried to attack her, and he believed his wife and threw Joseph into prison. I'm sure that wasn't like going to some kind of prison that we would go to today. I'm imagining it was very, very harsh.

So here we go again. Things were going so well and then suddenly Joseph is put in prison, probably facing a death sentence. He might have been tempted to say, "Why me? Why me, God? Why do these things keep happening to me? I'm doing what I'm supposed to be doing. I'm keeping the commandments. I'm working hard. I'm being a good person. Why does this keep happening to me?" But clearly he didn't do that. He didn't have that attitude. He had already learned that he just had to make the best of whatever happened and trust God to bring him safely through whatever the new challenge was.

This is to me one of the great examples from this story that many people often overlook. That even when bad things happen to us, we can take a positive approach, and if we do, it will actually improve everything for us. When we trust God and believe in him, it makes it much easier to stay positive in challenging or difficult times.

As the story goes along, Joseph becomes such a positive influence at the prison that the warden of the prison makes Joseph his helper. In the prison, he still is, so that's not great, but at least he's getting really good treatment in the prison because of his good attitude, his diligence, his intelligence, his hard work and so forth.

Then two other prisoners, the baker and the butler in Pharaoh's house, they've done something wrong and they've been put in prison. They have some really troubling dreams, and Joseph is able to interpret their dreams, and one of them is soon freed and goes back to work in Pharaoh's palace. Now, he had promised Joseph that he'd put in a good word for him, but he forgets all about him and doesn't say anything. But then the Pharaoh has a dream and that dream troubles him very much, and no one could interpret the dream, and the butler hears about this and remembers Joseph, and he tells the Pharaoh that there's this man in prison who can interpret dreams.

Well, you know the rest of the story. Joseph interprets the dream of Pharaoh. Pharaoh places Joseph in charge of everything in the kingdom. He becomes number two in all of Egypt, which is the most powerful country in all the area there at the time, and he's able to save the people of Egypt and save Pharaoh and all that he had, and he's even able to save his own family because the famine comes to the whole area, not just to Egypt.

In this powerful story we can see that many unfair and truly terrible things happen to Joseph, but Joseph doesn't give up on God. Despite all the pressures on his integrity or his sense of honor, he stays true to what he knows is right. To be specific, Joseph experienced three strong pressures on his integrity, pressures that we too will experience as our integrity is put to the test. The first of these pressures was the pull of the world. The world has different standards than we have. The second was the power of physical attraction. We all experience that. And the third was the peril of loneliness.

In the world today we often hear this lie: "Everybody's doing it. Why shouldn't I? Everybody's cheating. If I don't cheat, I won't get ahead." Things like that. Some people think that the only really important commandment is "thou shalt not get caught." The world's standards, however, stand in stark contrast to God's standards, and Joseph knew what God's standards were. And he wasn't willing to compromise them, no matter what the world said or did and no matter what happened to him.

Joseph was put in an impossible position. Would he lose his integrity or risk the wrath of his boss's wife? Look at what Joseph said when Potiphar's wife asked him to sleep with her: "How then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?" Joseph took a stand. We talk about awkward conversations—well, that was an awkward conversation. And he knew it was not going to end well for him, and he still had the awkward conversation. He still took the stand. He kept his integrity.

The second pressure on Joseph's integrity was the power of physical attraction. Joseph was obviously a good-looking man; otherwise, Potiphar's wife would not have tried to seduce him. Potiphar's wife was probably a beautiful woman. The fact of the matter was, this is something that a lot of people fall victim to. We live in a society where good looks are held in high esteem. Many of the stories in our newspapers and on the internet are about celebrities. They're not admired for their brains, but for their good looks. But God doesn't see his children that way.

Remember when the prophet Samuel was sent by God to anoint one of Jesse's sons as the new king in place of King Saul? He thought he was being sent to anoint Jesse's oldest son, a big, strong, good-looking man. But God said this to Samuel: "Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart." And so the young shepherd boy, David, was anointed the new king of Israel.

It's powerful for us to remember that in these pressures, Joseph was a model of standing up for what was right, even though it was going to end very, very badly for him. But there was another pressure, the third pressure, and that was the peril of loneliness. Loneliness can be a big problem in the world. It can be a big problem even in the church. Our church is heavily built around families, and singles can feel very left out at times. And disappointment and discouragement often accompany loneliness.

Joseph was alone in Egypt. He didn't even have a singles ward to go to. Joseph surely could have taken the easy way out so many times. He was lonely. He was alone. There was no one there to check up on him. Like you, he was away from his family. He had many opportunities to turn away from what he knew was right. But again, didn't matter whether it was in Potiphar's house, or in the prison, or in the caravan going to Egypt, or throughout his life—he simply didn't give in, even though not giving in would cost him his position, his freedom, and possibly his life.

However, as the scriptures tell us, the Lord was with Joseph. And the lesson for all of us is that God will always be with those who are faithful to him. Elders and sisters, let's all remember to be true to what we know is right, no matter what the pressures are that we feel. We love you.
